content.title: Will Artemis 2 return to Earth be visible in sky? What we know
content.text: With the Artemis II crew set to return to Earth later this week following their historic lunar voyage, would-be skywatchers may be wondering if the astronauts’ homecoming will be easily visible in the sky. Newsweek sought expert insight.Why It MattersThe mission’s four-strong crew lifted off on their manned test flight around the moon from the Kennedy Space Center in Florida’s Cape Canaveral on April 1.The journey has been record-breaking, with the crew eclipsing the record for the furthest human space flight earlier this week, traveling 248,655 miles from Earth and surpassing the record previously set by the Apollo 13 mission in 1970, NASA said.What To Know“The Orion spacecraft is planned to splash down on Friday afternoon in the Pacific Ocean near San Diego, a few minutes after 5 p.m. local time. While it will still be daytime, the sunlight in the west will make it difficult to observe with the naked eye, unfortunately,” Ehud Behar, an astrophysicist at the Technion–Israel Institute of Technology, told Newsweek.“However, weather is perhaps the most important factor to consider for visibility, especially when splashdown occurs far from shore," Behar said. "Based on a brief look at the forecast for that time, there is a chance that clouds will be coming in from the ocean, which would make observation impossible. Even haze and humidity can pose a challenge. If the weather gets too stormy, the splashdown could be delayed or moved to a new location entirely. We wouldn’t know if that is the case until only a few hours beforehand.”Artemis II lifts off from Launch Complex 39B at Kennedy Space Center on April 1, 2026, in Cape Canaveral, Florida. | Chip Somodevilla/Getty ImagesBehar said that nighttime conditions would significantly improve visibility during a splashdown. Unlike a launch, which unfolds gradually, the spacecraft’s initial descent happens very quickly. As it travels at high speed, heat buildup causes it to glow, potentially making it visible to observers who look up at the right moment. “If you catch a glimpse, the spacecraft will look like a slower-moving shooting star,” said Behar.“Regardless, NASA will likely be broadcasting the event from locations with much better visibility than anyone could hope to achieve on their own,” Behar added.A NASA spokesperson told Newsweek that the location and time of the Artemis II splashdown are “dynamic as mission milestones are reached."“In the days leading up to splashdown, updates will be available on NASA’s website and in our daily news conferences,” they added.What People Are SayingOrion crew member Christina Koch said during a Tuesday ship-to-ship call with the International Space Station: “The thing that changed for me looking back at Earth was I found myself noticing not only the beauty of the Earth but how much blackness there was around it. It just made it even more special."It truly emphasized how alike we are—how the same thing keeps every single person on planet Earth alive. We evolved on the same planet, we have shared things about how we love and live that are just universal, and the specialness and preciousness of that is emphasized when you realize how much else there is around it."
